title: Blessings, Warnings, and a Way Back
overview: At the close of the laws given at Sinai, God sets out what faithfulness will bring and what turning away will bring, and promises not to abandon Israel even in exile.

parts.label: Two core commands (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The laws are summed up in two key demands: make no carved images to bow down to, and keep the Sabbath rest days and honor the place of worship. This book often pairs these two because they kept Israel's worship centered on the LORD and away from other gods.

parts.label: Promises for faithfulness (vv. 3-13)
parts.note: Rain on time in autumn and spring would bring harvests so big that threshing grain ran into picking grapes, with peace and safety besides. The heart of it is God living among his people, which Christians later read as fulfilled in the church (2 Corinthians 6:16), and the broken yoke pictures slaves freed from Egypt now walking upright.

parts.label: Warnings that grow worse (vv. 14-26)
parts.note: If Israel breaks the covenant, the agreement binding them to God, troubles come in rising waves: disease, defeat, a drought where sky and ground turn hard as metal, wild animals, siege and famine. The repeated "seven times" means far more severe, and ten women baking in a single oven, with bread handed out by weight, shows desperate shortage.

parts.label: The worst case: ruin and exile (vv. 27-39)
parts.note: The text says plainly that starving people would eat their own children, a horror later recorded during the sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem, followed by ruined cities and shrines and scattering among other nations. The land would finally get the rest years Israel had skipped, every seventh year when fields were meant to lie unplanted (chapter 25), while survivors abroad would run at the sound of a blowing leaf.

parts.label: The door left open (vv. 40-45)
parts.note: If the exiles admit their wrongs and humble their "uncircumcised" hearts, meaning hearts closed off to God, he will remember his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Even in enemy lands he will not reject them completely or break his covenant with them.

parts.label: Closing summary (v. 46)
parts.note: This line rounds off the laws of Sinai as the terms of the relationship between the LORD and Israel, given through Moses.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these promises of material blessing and national restoration belong only to ancient Israel, apply in some form to believers today, or point to a future restoration of Israel still to come.
think: Is it easier for you to believe that wrongdoing brings real consequences, or that a badly broken relationship can still be repaired, and why?
